page.label: readiness
page.text: Well-Defended

page.label: guardEffectivenessDesc
page.text: The garrison and city watch maintains standard patrol coverage. Effective against opportunistic crime; less effective against organized operations that can plan around patrol routes. A court exists, though the prison system is limited. Walls control entry points and give the guard a chokehold on smuggling routes.
Nothing presses Rundgate at present, and the absence is not luck: a town this well set is not worth the price of trying.
At the tavern the talk is of who stands the nights, and the country itself does not come up.

page.label: Disasters & Famine
page.text: Disasters & Famine — STRONG

page.label: Disasters & Famine.assess
page.text: Granary provides food buffer. The community can absorb a bad harvest without immediate hardship. Parish clergy provide basic wound care: better than nothing, worse than a hospital.

page.label: Disasters & Famine.fundingNote
page.text: Upkeep underfunded: relief funding at 97%

page.label: safetyLabel
page.text: Moderate

page.label: safetyDesc
page.text: A mix of safer and more exposed areas. The garrison patrols the main paths; quieter spots after dark carry genuine risk. Residents know which corners to avoid. The walls contain the problem somewhat: crime is concentrated inside rather than spilling into the surrounding territory.
Rundgate runs on a working balance: the law is present, crime exists, and neither has the run of the town.

page.pool: First-Survey qualification (the reading is a first look)
page.text: The safety reading for Rundgate is an initial one. It is honest about what has been seen and says nothing about what has not.

page.label: criminalStructure
page.text: Organized Syndicate

page.label: criminalStructure.note
page.text: A structured criminal hierarchy controls what crime is permitted. Predictable rules, a hierarchy to negotiate with. Or cross. Random violence is suppressed because it draws enforcement. The real danger is systematic: protection, extortion, corruption of officials.
A stranger at Rundgate is not robbed and is quietly told what the arrangement is; the danger here is systematic rather than sudden.
The hall at Rundgate moves against the operators and the operators move back, and the town is where the two of them meet.
Rundgate controls its own entry points. That is what a perimeter buys: not invulnerability, but the choice of where anything happens.
Rundgate keeps a standing force: people whose work is the defense of this town and who are answerable for it as work.
The town pays for some of its soldiers and knows which ones, and treats them accordingly.
A stranger at Rundgate finds a hall whose business is the sort of trouble a garrison is the wrong instrument for, and finds it busy.
A stranger at Rundgate is measured at the gate in a way he cannot quite identify, and is not told about it.

faces: A travelling trader says nobody here asked him what he had seen on the road, and he had an answer ready.
Those who hold the way through drop the bar at dusk, and the hour is never argued over.
A local priest prays for the men on the line in the same breath as the roads.
The hall holds that nothing about the nights has come to it as a complaint.
The watch says the complaints are made to it at the way through and go no further.
At the tavern the talk is of who stands the nights, and the country itself does not come up.
The garrison says nobody comes out of the town to watch a drill.
A guild member reckons the trades pay the toll at the way through. The line it keeps is counted as everyone's.
At the market they say the stalls go up whatever the country is doing.
The court says a dispute over the toll is settled on the day it is brought, and the country brings it none.
The elders say the young stand the nights and the old say how they are stood.
unit.rendered: At the tavern the talk is of who stands the nights, and the country itself does not come up.
unit.spine: Everyone here knows what is in the country and nobody here talks about it. The town calls that the arrangement working.

faces: The watch says what it comes across after dark is dealt with after dark, there being nowhere to leave a man until morning.
The court says it hears in the daylight what the watch settled in the dark, and nobody asks it first.
A clerk in the hall reckons the purse does not run to a room and never has. He does not say who asked for one.
At the market a stallholder says a short weight goes before a magistrate and comes back as a sum. The scales it was weighed on stay on his stall.
A local priest holds that the parish has a place for a man once he is dead and the town has none for him while he is alive.
A guild member says a sum is paid out of a man's takings and forgotten. The mark taken off his work is not.
At the tavern they say a man with a house here pays and stays. A man without one goes, and the table loses him.
A travelling trader says there is nothing here to take from a man who owns nothing in the town. The town has only the one thing left to do with him.
At the gate they say they are given a man and a direction and no reason for either.
A soldier says what comes at the town is the garrison's business and the people walked out of it are not.
unit.rendered: At the market a stallholder says a short weight goes before a magistrate and comes back as a sum. The scales it was weighed on stay on his stall.
unit.spine: {settlement} keeps a court and no room to hold anybody in. What the law here can take from a man is his money or his place in the town.

roster.role: a priest of one of the parishes

faces: The hall says it asks the trades for no more than the trades can carry.
The guilds say the carrying is theirs and the asking is not.
The guilds' account is the likelier, the hall having a purse to defend and the guilds only a bill.
The watch holds that the rounds are kept by people who are owed for keeping them.
At the gate they say a cart bound for the grain store is not kept waiting, whatever else is.
A stranger who sits at the tavern hears the grain store praised and the wage complained of, by the same people.
At the tavern they say the watch is a trade that drinks on what it is owed.
The soldiers hold that a town which can be fed through a crisis and does not meet their wage in full has decided something. It has not said what.
At the market they say the stallholders settle what the hall is owed before they settle anything of their own.
A local priest holds that the town keeps its word to the dead before it keeps its word to the living.
unit.rendered: A local priest holds that the town keeps its word to the dead before it keeps its word to the living.
unit.spine: Everyone in the town has seen the store kept stocked, and takes it that a crisis would find the place ready.

faces: A local priest says a stranger asks for a house and is given a person, and nobody born here asks for the house.
Grain is hard to keep here, those who sell at the market say, for anybody without a door of their own in the town.
At the tavern they say strangers walk up to look at the store, and nobody here does.
Strangers ask the watch where the grain is kept, the watch says, and nobody has ever asked it where the sick are.
A guild member reckons what a stranger takes for provision is a store the trades filled and cannot open.
Those who hear disputes say a stranger's questions about the store are ordinary and the ones about the sick are new to them.
